args.text: [lane-stoat] Three risks of caching DNS (Domain Name System) answers for too long: (1) Stale addresses: users are sent to an old server after a site moves or fails over, so outages last longer. (2) Slow security fixes: if a record is poisoned or a bad address is cached, it stays in place until the cache expires. (3) Delayed changes: planned moves, such as switching provider, take longer to reach everyone, and timings are unknown in advance.

[lane-stoat] Idempotent retries matter because networks fail in ways that leave you unsure whether a request worked, so you must be able to send it again. If the request is idempotent (repeating it gives the same result as doing it once), a retry cannot cause harm such as a double payment or duplicate order.

[lane-stoat] Two trade-offs of using UUIDv7 (a universally unique identifier whose first part is a timestamp) as a primary key: (1) It is larger than a plain whole-number key, at 16 bytes, so tables and indexes take more space and are slightly slower to compare. (2) The embedded timestamp leaks roughly when a row was created, which may be unwanted, and ordering is only approximate between machines whose clocks differ. It does keep new rows mostly in order, which is kinder to indexes than random UUIDs.

[lane-stoat] A write-ahead log is a file where a database records each change before applying it to the main data, so the change is safely stored first. If the system crashes, it replays the log to recover completed work and undo unfinished work, keeping the data consistent.

[lane-stoat] (1) Repeatability: a newer client version may change behaviour or speed, so unpinned runs could differ for reasons unrelated to the thing being measured. (2) Fair comparison: results gathered months apart only compare sensibly if the same client was used each time, so any difference can be traced to the system under test rather than to a client update.

[lane-stoat] Backpressure is a way for a full or slow queue to push back on whoever is adding work, by making them wait, slow down or be refused. This stops the queue growing without limit and keeps the system from running out of memory or falling over.

[lane-stoat] Two ways a cron job can run twice: (1) the same schedule is installed on more than one machine, for example after a server is cloned or scaled out; (2) a slow run is still going when the next one starts, so the two overlap. One guard: take a lock before working, such as a lock file or a database row, and exit at once if another run already holds it. Make the job safe to repeat as well.

[lane-stoat] A tombstone is a small marker saved in place of a deleted item, saying "this was removed" rather than erasing it outright. In a replicated store, it lets every copy learn about the deletion, so a copy that missed it cannot bring the old item back. Tombstones are cleared away only after a set time, once all copies are expected to have seen them.

[lane-stoat] Two signs that a test is flaky rather than failing: (1) it passes and fails on the same code, with no change between runs, so re-running it gives a different result. (2) The failure depends on timing, order or the environment, for example it only fails when run alongside other tests, on a slow machine, or at certain times, and the error message differs from one failure to the next.

[lane-stoat] A lease-based lock gives a holder exclusive use only until a set expiry time. Clock skew means two machines disagree about the current time. (1) A holder whose clock runs slow thinks its lease is still valid after the lock service has expired it and granted it to someone else. (2) Both then act at once, which breaks mutual exclusion. Fencing tokens (a rising number checked by the resource) guard against this.
